title: Assessment of Cardiovascular Status
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Cardiovascular Disorders

headings.title: Introduction to Cardiovascular Assessment in Midwifery
headings.content: During pregnancy and the postpartum period, the maternal cardiovascular system undergoes profound physiological adaptations. Blood volume increases by up to forty percent, cardiac output rises, and systemic vascular resistance drops. These changes support the growing uteroplacental unit but also place significant strain on the heart. Midwives must assess cardiovascular status routinely to distinguish normal pregnancy changes from pathological conditions like pre-existing heart disease, peripartum cardiomyopathy, or hypertensive disorders. Baseline assessment during the first antenatal visit establishes a reference point for detecting subtle deviations later in gestation.

headings.title: Comprehensive History Taking and Risk Identification
headings.content: A thorough cardiovascular history uncovers hidden risks that physical exams alone might miss. Midwives must screen for a personal or family history of rheumatic heart disease, congenital heart defects, hypertension, and venous thromboembolism. Direct questioning should target specific symptoms such as progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, chest pain, palpitations, and unexplained syncope. In many Nigerian communities, traditional remedies or self-medication should also be asked about gently, as some herbs affect blood pressure and heart rate. Identifying these risk factors early allows for timely referral to a physician or cardiologist.

headings.title: Systematic Physical Examination Techniques
headings.content: Physical examination of the cardiovascular system follows a structured clinical sequence: inspection, palpation, and auscultation. Midwives begin by observing the general appearance, skin color for cyanosis or pallor, and the neck veins for jugular venous distension. Palpation focuses on feeling the peripheral pulses for rate, rhythm, and volume, alongside locating the apex beat on the chest wall. The patient should be positioned comfortably, usually sitting upright or tilted slightly to the left to prevent supine hypotension syndrome when checking the precordium.

headings.title: Auscultating Heart Sounds and Identifying Abnormalities
headings.content: Using the diaphragm and bell of the stethoscope, midwives listen across specific anatomical areas: aortic, pulmonic, tricuspid, and mitral valves. Normal heart sounds include S1 (closure of AV valves) and S2 (closure of semilunar valves). Due to increased blood flow, a soft systolic murmur is common and normal in pregnancy. However, loud murmurs, diastolic murmurs, or the presence of an S3 or S4 gallop rhythm require expert evaluation. Midwives must learn to distinguish these benign physiological sounds from pathological murmurs that suggest structural heart disease.

headings.title: Evaluating Peripheral Circulation and Edema
headings.content:
Assessing peripheral circulation involves checking capillary refill time, skin temperature, and peripheral pulse strength in the upper and lower extremities. Midwives also inspect the limbs for dependent edema, which is common in late pregnancy due to increased venous pressure in the lower legs. Pitting edema is assessed by pressing a finger firmly against the bony prominence of the tibia or medial malleolus for several seconds. 

- **Grade 1+**: Mild pitting, slight indentation with no perceptible swelling.
- **Grade 2+**: Moderate pitting, indentation subsides rapidly.
- **Grade 3+**: Deep pitting, indentation remains for a short time.
- **Grade 4+**: Very deep pitting, indentation lasts a long time and limbs look swollen.

While mild ankle edema can be normal after standing, generalized edema involving the face and hands is a red flag for pre-eclampsia.

headings.title: Diagnostic Investigations and Interpretation
headings.content: When clinical assessments reveal abnormalities, midwives collaborate with medical colleagues to utilize diagnostic tools. The standard 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) evaluates cardiac electrical activity and detects arrhythmias or ventricular hypertrophy. Obstetric ultrasonography paired with echocardiography provides direct visualization of heart valves and chamber sizes without radiation risks. Routine antenatal blood tests also supply vital clues; for instance, complete blood counts reveal anemia, which forces the heart to work harder and can precipitate heart failure in vulnerable women.

headings.title: Documenting and Monitoring Cardiovascular Status
headings.content: Accurate documentation ensures continuity of care across different shifts and healthcare providers. Midwives must record baseline vitals, exact locations and grades of murmurs, edema scores, and patient-reported symptoms in the antenatal or clinical record. Ongoing monitoring schedules should be tailored to the individual risk level; women with diagnosed heart conditions require frequent reassessment during labor and the immediate postpartum period, which is a time of dramatic hemodynamic shifts. Clear communication and detailed records protect both the patient and the healthcare team.
